Live page text: UX Case Study: Odysseyware Virtual Science Labs Overview Role & Scope Constraints Process & Flow Outcomes & Reflection UX Case Study Odysseyware Virtual Science Labs Translating physical classrooms into intuitive digital experiences. Bridging the gap between tactile science experiments and scalable LMS architecture. Role Sr. UX Designer Timeline 2014 2016 Platform Web / Mobile Responsive Deliverable End-to-End Product Design Project Context & Scope Odysseyware required a modern, scalable solution to bring 20 high-fidelity virtual science labs (covering subjects from Osmosis and Circuitry to Frog Dissection) into their existing ecosystem. Team & Leadership I led end-to-end design, directing a team of junior designers while establishing tight cross-functional alignment with Subject Matter Experts (SMEs), Instructional Designers, Curriculum Writers, QA engineers, and the VP of Product. My Scope My responsibilities spanned from initial problem/solution alignment and Information Architecture (IA) to detailed wireframes, UI specifications, and delivering fully functional prototypes ready for the engineeri

gnment and Information Architecture (IA) to detailed wireframes, UI specifications, and delivering fully functional prototypes ready for the engineering handoff. Challenges & Constraints Translating Physical to Digital The core challenge was recreating real-world, hands-on labs (e.g., frog dissections, mechanical physics) in a way that felt authentic to a classroom setting. The digital interface needed to be highly intuitive and engaging for students in varying grades, without abstracting away the learning objectives of the physical experiment. Managing Cognitive Load Leveraging behavioral UX principles like Hick's Law, I designed the interface strictly from a student’s curious perspective, paired with instructor oversight. It was critical that students weren't overwhelmed by competing UI elements—toolsets, simulation mechanics, anatomy overlays, and educational text had to be progressively disclosed. Technical & LMS Constraints The solution required responsive and reactive layouts to render flawlessly across desktop and mobile devices. Additionally, strict constraints imposed by the Odysseyware LMS framework required complex user states: authentication protocols, audit trails, and

s. Additionally, strict constraints imposed by the Odysseyware LMS framework required complex user states: authentication protocols, audit trails, and specific checks and balances to validate accurate interactions for both students and teachers. Evolution of the Interface Interactive comparison: Wireframe vs. High-Fidelity Render. Drag the slider to compare. --> --> Design Process & Solutions Information Architecture Key Feature UX Testing & Iteration Structuring the Student Journey The ecosystem required a seamless transition logic. I architected user flows where a student would intuitively navigate from a standard lesson module directly into a virtual lab environment, perform the experiential task, and transition flawlessly into built-in assessments. The architecture supported repeating virtual labs asynchronously as needed for study or remediation. Interaction Paradigms Creating realism without physical touch required specific interaction models. I designed UX logic to incorporate precision clicking/drag-and-drop mechanics for biological dissections, real-time reactive data tracking UI for physics labs, and persistent, immediate feedback loops for progress tracking so students a

ogical dissections, real-time reactive data tracking UI for physics labs, and persistent, immediate feedback loops for progress tracking so students always understood their context within the experiment. Validating with the Classroom I led cross-functional workshops and conducted direct usability testing with actual target students, while consulting real classroom science teachers as subject matter experts. The major UX pivots and interface refinements we executed prior to launch were directly informed by observing how students naturally interpreted (or misinterpreted) digital tools compared to physical ones. Outcomes & Reflections The Reception Upon release, the UX was received with overwhelming enthusiasm by educators and students alike. The success of the initial 20 modules validated the architectural approach, driving executive buy-in for further expansion and the commissioning of new virtual science content. Address

# Tangible DLS

A React design language system indexed to the [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/installation) documentation map.

It is not a copy of the Tailwind docs, and it is not affiliated with Tailwind Labs. Every current docs group is here — getting started, core concepts, base styles, layout, flexbox and grid, spacing, sizing, typography, backgrounds, borders, effects, filters, tables, transitions and animation, transforms, interactivity, SVG, and accessibility — with original explanations, the naming rule for each scale, and a live specimen.

On top of that map is the part a product team actually imports: tokens in CSS, and a small set of React components (button, badge, card, field, alert, avatar, switch).

## Stack

React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, Vite. One package. “Mono” here means a single React library, not a multi-package workspace. Split it into `packages/ui` when you publish to npm — not before the API settles.

## Run

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open a topic with `/?topic=flex-direction`. Components live at `/?topic=components`.

```tsx
import { Button, Field

`bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open a topic with `/?topic=flex-direction`. Components live at `/?topic=components`.

```tsx
import { Button, Field, Card } from "@/dls/ui";
```

Tokens live in `src/styles.css` under `@theme`. Utilities read those variables, so light and dark are one class set.

## What was deliberately left out

- A verbatim mirror of tailwindcss.com. Their prose is theirs. This repo links to the official page from each topic.
- Every numeric step of every scale. `p-0` through `p-96` is a rule, not 80 near-duplicate rows. The rule is on the page.
- Framework install guides (Next, Rails, Laravel). This repo is the Vite + React path. Other stacks stay on the official installation pages.

## License

MIT for the code in this repository. Tailwind CSS is published under its own license.

## What Changed

- **Color palette** — Apple system colors: `#007AFF` blue, `#34C759` green, `#FF3B30` red, `#FF9500` orange, `#AF52DE` purple — no custom brand tints

# Gemini Job Bot

Upload a resume PDF → Gemini extracts job titles → Serper searches → verified job board filter → clean list of real listings.

## Setup

1. Clone repo
2. `npm install`
3. Copy `.env.local.example` to `.env.local` and add your keys:
   - `GEMINI_API_KEY`
   - `SERPER_API_KEY`
4. `npm run dev`

## Deploy to Vercel

1. Connect repo in Vercel dashboard
2. Add env vars: `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `SERPER_API_KEY`
3. Deploy

## Order of Operations

1. User uploads PDF
2. `/api/extract` → pdf-parse → Gemini structured JSON → job titles + seniority
3. `/api/search` → Serper searches each title → full raw list
4. URL filter against `lib/jobBoardAllowlist.ts` (60+ verified domains)
5. Verified jobs returned with title, company, description, apply link

# CMSPayload — Payload UI Catalog

An interactive catalog of the Payload CMS admin UI (`packages/ui`, v4.0.0-beta.0 source):

- **190 components** (157 elements + 33 fields) — every one with its full source (`.tsx`, `.ts`, `.css`), syntax highlighted, with **Copy file** and **Copy all for AI** buttons.
- **94 interactive previews** (hand-built, many with variant controls), **81 stand-in previews** auto-assembled from each component's own CSS classes, and **15 items marked “Logic only, nothing to display”** (background helpers with no visual).
- **Theme / rebrand panel** (`/theme`): edit any Payload CSS variable (colors, radius, spacing, typography), presets, light/dark mode, and export the overrides as `custom.css` for your Payload app.

## How it works

- `payload-src/` — a copy of `packages/ui/src/{elements,fields,icons,css}` from the Payload monorepo.
- `scripts/prepare.mjs` (runs automatically before `dev`/`build`) generates:
  - `public/payload-ui.css` — Payload's real stylesheet (tokens + every component CSS)
  - `src/generated/catalog.json` — the component list + source files

ublic/payload-ui.css` — Payload's real stylesheet (tokens + every component CSS)
  - `src/generated/catalog.json` — the component list + source files
- Live previews (`src/components/Previews.tsx`) render the same DOM/BEM classes as Payload's components, styled by Payload's real CSS. They are lightweight re-implementations, so they run without Payload's config, i18n, form state or a database. Components that need the full Payload runtime are listed **source only**.

To refresh from a newer Payload checkout, replace `payload-src/` with the new `packages/ui/src` folders (`elements fields icons css styles.css`) and rebuild.

## Run locally

```bash
npm install
npm run dev        # http://localhost:3000
npm run build && npm start   # production
```

Requires Node 18.18+ (20+ recommended).

## Push to GitHub

```bash
git init
git add .
git commit -m "CMSPayload: Payload UI catalog"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/<you>/CMSPayload.git
git push -u origin main
```

Open a component → **Copy all for AI** → paste into your AI tool with a prompt like
“Using this Payload UI component as reference, create a `PlexusStatCard` that uses the same CSS variables and BEM conventions.”
Add the result as a new preview in `src/components/Previews.tsx` (and its key in `previewKeys.ts`).

## Note on `payload-src`

In the GitHub repo, the Payload source is stored as a single file, `payload-src.bundle.json`. `npm run dev` / `npm run build` unpack it to `payload-src/` automatically (the folder is git-ignored). To update it from a new Payload checkout, replace `payload-src/` and regenerate the bundle with:

# Design Operations Guide

The authoritative operational reference for the eCommerce site, Customer Portal, and Back Office product cycle — covering all 11 sections, DRAC accountability model, and full tool configuration for Jira, Confluence, and Workfront.

---

## Deploy to Vercel (recommended)

### From GitHub (auto-deploy on every push)

1. Push this repo to GitHub (public or private)
2. Go to [vercel.com](https://vercel.com) → **Add New Project**
3. Import your GitHub repo
4. Vercel auto-detects Vite — no configuration needed
5. Click **Deploy**

Every push to `main` triggers an automatic redeploy.

### From Vercel CLI

```bash
npm install -g vercel
vercel
```

---

## Run locally

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:5173

---

## Project structure

```
designops-guide/
├── index.html          # HTML entry point
├── vite.config.js      # Vite + React config
├── vercel.json         # Vercel deployment config
├── package.json        # React 18 + Vite 5
├── .gitignore
├── README.md
└── src/
    ├── main.jsx        # React root (mounts App)
    └── App.jsx

├── package.json        # React 18 + Vite 5
├── .gitignore
├── README.md
└── src/
    ├── main.jsx        # React root (mounts App)
    └── App.jsx         # Entire application — all 11 sections
```

---

## Stack

- **React 18** — UI
- **Vite 5** — build tool and dev server  
- **Zero external UI dependencies** — all styles inline, no CSS files, no UI libraries

---

## Editing content

All content, styles, and logic live in `src/App.jsx`. To update a section, find the relevant object in the `SECTIONS` array at the top of the file, edit the data, save, and push. Vercel redeploys automatically.
